title: How to Learn Online (Skills for Learning)

lessons.title: Skills that help you learn
lessons.html:
The Government of Canada’s Skills for Success model describes skills that help people in work, learning, and life. The official page says these skills help you get a job, progress at work, change jobs, take part in your community, and succeed in learning. They are for everyone — not only students in a full-time school.

Three of those skills matter a great deal when you learn online:

  • Adaptability — reaching or adjusting your goals when things change, by planning, staying focused, persisting, and overcoming setbacks. Official examples include learning how to use new tools and improving through feedback.
  • Digital — using digital technology to find, manage, apply, create, and share information. Official examples include using common devices and tools, storing files, and practising safe habits online.
  • Problem solving — identifying an issue, gathering information, thinking of options, and learning from the result. The official list includes asking other people for help when you need it.

In Alberta, the government’s Community Adult Learning Program (CALP) funds local organizations that offer part-time, non-formal learning close to where you live. Alberta.ca says those providers may help with literacy, numeracy, English language skills, basic digital skills, and skills for learning, in safe and welcoming places.

This short course is itself practice: you will set a goal, plan a study time, and try digital habits. It does not replace a tutor or a longer program, and the certificate at the end is completion only.

If a word on a website is new, write it down and ask council staff.

lessons.title: Set a goal and a simple plan
lessons.html:
Skills for Success says adaptability includes setting or adjusting goals based on your skills, resources, and supports, and planning and prioritizing: define tasks and milestones, then choose an order that fits your situation.

Alberta’s official careers site, alis, says studying well takes motivation, organization, time, and practice — including when you also have work and family responsibilities. Alis suggests:

  • Set realistic long-term and short-term goals (for example, finish two lessons this week), not only a far-away finish line.
  • Write due dates and plans on a calendar, agenda book, phone, or other tool you will actually look at.
  • Make monthly and weekly plans and a daily to-do list.
  • Keep the schedule flexible. Unexpected events happen. Review the plan and change it when you need to.
  • Do not “steal” from study time if you can help it. Alis suggests using small bits of found time (waiting, travel) if you need more minutes.

Another alis page, written for adults going back to learning, adds: decide what is most important, put everything in one calendar, set deadlines for each task, and give yourself a small reward when you finish on time. It also says you will be happier and more successful if you let go of the need to be perfect.

Alberta.ca’s “Going back to school as an adult” page asks you to think first: Why am I learning? What do I need to learn? How do I learn best? Online study on a computer is one of the ways it lists, along with a classroom, a tutor, or correspondence.

Try this now: write one goal for this course and the day and time you will do the next lesson.

lessons.title: Study habits that fit adult life
lessons.html:
Alis says shorter, regular study periods work better than long “marathon” sessions, and that frequent breaks help. On its “How to Study Effectively” page, alis suggests planning a short break every 50 minutes or so. If you study longer than two hours, try switching to a different subject every hour. Study at the time of day when you are most alert when you can. Studying when you are exhausted or distracted is much harder.

On “Fitting Everything In,” alis suggests frequent short study periods and, when you must study longer, a 15-minute break for every 60 to 90 minutes of study time. Leave some flexibility for unexpected demands. Aim for balance: eat properly, rest, and get some exercise.

To make it easier to start, alis recommends:

  • a quiet place with a table or desk, a comfortable chair, and good lighting
  • tools you need kept handy
  • shorter but more frequent sessions if it is hard to focus at first

To avoid putting work off (procrastinating), alis says to notice excuses such as “it can wait” or “I’ll just finish this show first,” and to break large tasks into smaller ones you can finish in a short time.

Skills for Success adaptability adds everyday actions that match those tips: focus on the current task, minimize distractions, and manage your time (for example, be on time and do not waste time). Persist when something does not go as planned, or change your approach when that is the wiser choice.

You do not need a special app to use these habits. A paper list and a quiet corner of the table can be enough.

lessons.title: Digital habits for an online course
lessons.html:
Skills for Success describes digital skill as using technology to find, manage, apply, create, and share information. Official components that help in an online course include:

  • Using common devices (a computer, tablet, or smartphone) and knowing basic on-screen actions.
  • Navigating a page: scrolling, using Back and Next, and knowing which part of a site to open.
  • Using search to find information (for example, a search box on a page).
  • Storing and organizing files in folders with clear names, such as saving a worksheet into a “Courses” folder.
  • Using online forms (signing in, quizzes, applications).
  • Practising safe habits: create a password to protect your information, know what personal details you should not share, and be careful with risky messages.

Do not type your real course password into this lesson. If you learn on a shared computer, sign out when you finish.

If an email or pop-up asks for a password or a gift-card payment to “unlock” a lesson, stop. That is not how this course works. See also Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada for phishing and scam messages. Skills for Success specifically lists knowing how to avoid phishing emails as part of safe digital practice.

When information on the internet disagrees, Skills for Success reading skill says to think about whether an online source is relevant and trustworthy. Prefer official pages (such as Canada.ca or Alberta.ca) for rules and government programs.

If a button or video will not open, write down what you clicked and ask council staff. That is problem solving, not failure.

lessons.title: When you get stuck, and where to get help
lessons.html:
Everyone gets stuck sometimes. Skills for Success says adaptability includes identifying when to keep trying and when to change your approach, learning from setbacks and mistakes, and staying calm enough to continue. Problem solving includes gathering information, breaking a problem into smaller parts, and seeking help from others if needed.

Alis says that if you need help with study skills — for example, how to take notes or remember what you read — you can ask about resources at the place you are learning or speak with a librarian. On the same pages, alis lists the Alberta Supports Contact Centre at 1-877-644-9992 (toll free).

In Alberta you can also:

  • Ask staff at your adult learning council (many are Community Adult Learning Program providers). Alberta.ca says about 80 organizations offer these local opportunities. The CALP overview page includes a link to find a provider near you.
  • Read Going back to school as an adult on Alberta.ca for classroom, tutor, correspondence, and online options, including literacy, numeracy, English, digital skills, and life skills. That page says Alberta Supports can help if you are not sure which program fits, and it lists the Foundational Learning and Skills Development Unit (toll free 1-800-222-6485, weekdays).

This course cannot choose a program or funding for you, and it is not a promise of a job or a diploma.

If a lesson feels too hard, pause, review the official source link, try a smaller piece, then ask a person. That is learning.
